questions.stem:
A circular coil of 5 turns and radius 6.0 cm lies in the plane of the paper. A magnetic field acts perpendicularly into the paper as shown.

The magnetic flux density of the magnetic field changes in magnitude from 0.75 T to 0.18 T in 0.42 s.

What is the average e.m.f. induced in the coil?
questions.stemText: A circular coil of 5 turns and radius 6.0 cm lies in the plane of the paper. A magnetic field acts perpendicularly into the paper as shown. x x x x x x magnetic field into plane of paper x x x x x x x x x x x x x x x x x x coil of 5 turns x x x x x x x x x x x x The magnetic flux density of the magnetic field changes in magnitude from 0.75 T to 0.18 T in 0.42 s. What is the average e.m.f. induced in the coil? A 15 mV B 72 mV C 77 mV D 96 mV

options.label: A
options.text: 15 mV

options.label: B
options.text: 72 mV

options.label: C
options.text: 77 mV

options.label: D
options.text: 96 mV

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Direct use of Faraday's law with flux linkage $NBA$.
questions.misconception: Forgetting the number of turns or using diameter/final B only

explanation.body: Faraday’s law gives the magnitude of the average induced e.m.f. as $\mathcal{E}=NA|\Delta B|/\Delta t$. Substitution gives $\mathcal{E}=\frac{5\pi(0.060)^2}{0.42}(0.75-0.18)=0.0767\ \mathrm{V}$, or $77\ \mathrm{mV}$.

perOption.A: Calculates the e.m.f. for one turn.
perOption.B: Uses a flux-density change smaller than 0.57 T or an equivalent underestimate of the flux-linkage change.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Overestimates the ratio of the flux-linkage change to the elapsed time.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A 100% efficient transformer is connected as shown to a sinusoidal a.c. supply.

What is the reading on the ammeter?
questions.stemText: A 100% efficient transformer is connected as shown to a sinusoidal a.c. supply. primary coil secondary coil 200 turns 1000 turns A output a.c. supply 100  80 V a.c. What is the reading on the ammeter? A 0.16 A B 0.80 A C 2.8 A D 4.0 A

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Find secondary current, then use the turns ratio for an ideal transformer.
questions.misconception: Inverting the current ratio of a transformer (current steps the opposite way to voltage)

explanation.body: The secondary current is $I_s=V_s/R=80/100=0.80\ \mathrm{A}$. For the ideal transformer, $I_p/I_s=N_s/N_p$, so $I_p=(1000/200)(0.80)=4.0\ \mathrm{A}$.

perOption.A: Inverts the current ratio.
perOption.B: Uses the secondary current as the ammeter reading.
perOption.C: Divides by the peak-to-r.m.s. factor even though the given a.c. voltage is already r.m.s.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.stem:
The North pole of a bar magnet is pushed into a coil of wire from end X. The maximum movement of the meter needle is 10 units to the left.

In a similar set up, the South pole of the magnet is pushed into a coil of wire from end X at half the speed.

What is the maximum movement of the meter needle?

X S N In a similar set up, the South pole of the magnet is pushed into a coil of wire from end X at half the speed. What is the maximum movement of the meter needle? A less than 10 units to the left B less than 10 units to the right C more than 10 units to the left D more than 10 units to the right

options.text: less than 10 units to the left

options.label: B

options.label: D
options.text: more than 10 units to the right

questions.difficultyReason: Qualitative application of Faraday's and Lenz's laws to reversed pole and lower speed.
questions.misconception: Forgetting that reversing the pole reverses the induced current, or that the size depends on rate of change of flux

explanation.body: By Lenz's law the coil end X becomes a north pole when north approaches and a south pole when south approaches, reversing the current and the needle deflection. At half the speed, the flux linkage changes more slowly, so the induced e.m.f. and current are smaller.

perOption.A: Accounts for the smaller deflection but misses the reversal caused by switching poles.
perOption.B: Correct. The needle moves less than 10 units to the right.
perOption.C: Misses both the current reversal and the decrease in magnitude.
perOption.D: Gets the reversal right but treats slower insertion as producing a larger current.

questions.difficultyReason: Requires the force on charges in a moving conductor and the source-versus-load sign of potential.
questions.misconception: Assuming current flows from high to low potential inside the source (the disc) as it does in the external resistor

explanation.body: Treat PQ as a straight conductor moving in the magnetic field. Fleming's right-hand rule gives conventional current from P to Q along the disc. The rotating disc acts as a source, so current flows internally from lower to higher potential and P is at lower potential than Q.

perOption.A: Correct. The disc drives current from P to Q with Q at higher potential.
perOption.B: Gets the polarity right but reverses the current inside the source.
perOption.C: Reverses both the induced current and the polarity.
perOption.D: Gets the current direction right but applies a resistor's potential drop to the source.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A straight metal rod XY of length 24 cm moves at a constant velocity of 0.50 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ along a very long metal frame. The rod is moved in a region of uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.15 T directed into the plane of the frame throughout its entire length.

What is the magnitude of the magnetic flux cut by the rod in half a minute?
questions.stemText: A straight metal rod XY of length 24 cm moves at a constant velocity of 0.50 m s-1 along a very long metal frame. The rod is moved in a region of uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.15 T directed into the plane of the frame throughout its entire length. What is the magnitude of the magnetic flux cut by the rod in half a minute? A 0.018 Wb B 0.036 Wb C 0.54 Wb D 1.1 Wb

appearances.originalFile: CJC PHY/H2/J2.H2.PRELIM.2026.Paper 1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Direct use of flux cut $= BLvt$ with unit conversions.
questions.misconception: Forgetting to convert minutes to seconds or cm to m

explanation.body: The flux cut is $\Delta\Phi=BA=BL(vt)$. In $30\ \mathrm{s}$, the rod sweeps out $A=0.24(0.50\times30)=3.6\ \mathrm{m^2}$. The flux cut is therefore $0.15\times3.6=0.54\ \mathrm{Wb}$.

perOption.A: Gives the flux cut in one second.
perOption.B: Gives the flux cut in two seconds.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses a full minute instead of half a minute.

[Diagram: horizontal field lines to the right; coil originally vertical (plane perpendicular to field), new position tilted at an angle.] The coil is rotated to the new position shown. How do the magnetic flux density and the total magnetic flux through the coil change during the rotation? A decrease, decrease B increase, increase C no change, decrease D no change, increase

questions.difficultyReason: Simple recognition that the field is unchanged while the perpendicular area decreases.
questions.misconception: Confusing magnetic flux density with magnetic flux

explanation.body: The magnetic flux density $B$ stays constant because the external field is unaffected by the rotation. The initial flux is maximal, and the tilt reduces the area projected perpendicular to the field, so the flux decreases.

perOption.A: Confuses the decreasing component normal to the coil with a decrease in the field magnitude.
perOption.B: Assumes rotation strengthens the external field and increases the flux.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Assumes the flux increases as the coil tilts away from its maximum-flux orientation.

questions.stem: A coil produces a magnetic flux of 0.85 Wb. A second coil of 1500 turns is wound on the same core, such that all the magnetic flux from the first coil links the second coil. What is the e.m.f. induced across the terminals of the second coil when the flux produced by the first coil is reduced uniformly to zero in 0.19 s?
questions.stemText: A coil produces a magnetic flux of 0.85 Wb. A second coil of 1500 turns is wound on the same core, such that all the magnetic flux from the first coil links the second coil. What is the e.m.f. induced across the terminals of the second coil when the flux produced by the first coil is reduced uniformly to zero in 0.19 s? A 0 V B 4.47 V C 335 V D 6710 V

options.label: A
options.text: 0 V

appearances.originalFile: DHS Physics Prelim 2026/H2/DHS 2026 Y6 Physics H2 P1 Prelim (for external sharing).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Direct application of Faraday's law with flux linkage.
questions.misconception: Forgetting to multiply by the number of turns

explanation.body: By Faraday's law, the magnitude of the induced e.m.f. is $|\mathcal E|=N|\Delta\Phi|/\Delta t$. With $1500$ turns and a flux change of $0.85\ \mathrm{Wb}$ in $0.19\ \mathrm s$, this gives $1500(0.85/0.19)\approx6711\ \mathrm V\approx6710\ \mathrm V$.

perOption.A: Uses the zero final flux in place of the nonzero change in flux.
perOption.B: Calculates the induced e.m.f. for one turn only.
perOption.C: Underestimates the rate of change of flux linkage across all 1500 turns.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A coplanar U-shaped wire PQ moves in a uniform magnetic field in the direction shown. The plane of the wire is perpendicular to the magnetic field.

The variation with time t of the displacement s of the wire is shown.

Which graph represents the electromotive force E induced across the wire PQ?
questions.stemText: A coplanar U-shaped wire PQ moves in a uniform magnetic field in the direction shown. The plane of the wire is perpendicular to the magnetic field. P Q magnetic field into the U-shaped plane of paper wire The variation with time t of the displacement s of the wire is shown. s 0 t 0 Which graph represents the electromotive force E induced across the wire PQ? A E 0 t 0 B E 0 t 0 C E D E

appearances.originalFile: JPJC PHYSICS/H2/2026 Prelim H2 Phy P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Students must see that the two arm e.m.f.s cancel, despite the motion graph pointing towards a velocity-shaped answer.
questions.misconception: Treating the e.m.f. across PQ as proportional to the velocity of the wire

explanation.body: The left vertical arm moves across the field, making P positive relative to the bottom of that arm. The horizontal arm moves along its length, so it develops no e.m.f. along the wire. The right arm develops the same e.m.f. as the left arm, making Q positive by the same amount. P and Q therefore stay at the same potential throughout the motion in the uniform field.

perOption.A: This assigns a nonzero terminal e.m.f. at the ends of the motion even though the arm e.m.f.s cancel.
perOption.B: Changing speed changes both arm e.m.f.s equally, so there are no terminal pulses.
perOption.C: Correct. The terminal e.m.f. stays zero.
perOption.D: This follows the speed as if only one vertical arm contributed to the terminal e.m.f.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: Which two features are necessary for the operation of a transformer? [Table: feature one / feature two] A electrical connection between primary and secondary coils / input of direct current. B magnetic interaction between primary and secondary coils / input of direct current. C electrical connection between primary and secondary coils / input of alternating current. D magnetic interaction between primary and secondary coils / input of alternating current.

stemImage.alt: Question 26: Which two features are necessary for the operation of a transformer? feature one feature two

appearances.originalFile: JPJC PHYSICS/H2/2026 Prelim H2 Phy P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Direct recall of how a transformer works.
questions.misconception: Thinking a transformer passes current through a wire connection or works with d.c.

explanation.body: A transformer couples the primary and secondary coils through a shared magnetic field, usually guided by a soft iron core. An alternating current in the primary produces a changing magnetic flux linkage in the secondary, inducing an e.m.f. by Faraday’s law.

perOption.A: The coils couple magnetically, and steady direct current produces a constant flux after switch-on.
perOption.B: Magnetic coupling is required, but steady direct current cannot sustain a changing flux.
perOption.C: Alternating current supplies the changing flux, but the coupling between the coils is magnetic.
perOption.D: Correct. Alternating current produces the changing flux needed for mutual induction.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: The primary of an ideal transformer has 200 turns and is connected to a $25\ \mathrm{V}$ r.m.s. alternating current supply. The secondary has 1600 turns and is connected to a resistor of resistance $150\ \Omega$, as shown below. [Diagram: transformer with 200-turn primary connected to $25\ \mathrm{V}$ a.c. r.m.s. and 1600-turn secondary connected to a $150\ \Omega$ resistor] What are the possible values of the secondary voltage, the secondary current and the mean power dissipated in the resistor? A $3.1\ \mathrm{V}$, $0.021\ \mathrm{A}$, $0.065\ \mathrm{W}$ B $25\ \mathrm{V}$, $0.17\ \mathrm{A}$, $4.2\ \mathrm{W}$ C $200\ \mathrm{V}$, $1.3\ \mathrm{A}$, $270\ \mathrm{W}$ D $200\ \mathrm{V}$, $1.3\ \mathrm{A}$, $530\ \mathrm{W}$

stemImage.alt: Question 21: The primary of an ideal transformer has 200 turns and is connected to a 25 V r.m.s. alternating current supply. The secondary has 1600 turns and is connected to

appearances.originalFile: NJC/H2 Physics/NJC_2026_H2_Physics_Prelim_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Turns ratio then Ohm's law and power with r.m.s. values.
questions.misconception: Using the peak-power doubling or inverting the turns ratio

explanation.body: The turns ratio gives the secondary r.m.s. voltage $V_S=(1600/200)(25)=200\ \mathrm{V}$. Ohm’s law gives the secondary r.m.s. current $200/150=1.333\ \mathrm{A}$. The mean resistor power is $V_S^2/R=200^2/150=266.7\ \mathrm{W}$, which rounds to $270\ \mathrm{W}$.

perOption.A: Inverts the turns ratio and predicts a step-down.
perOption.B: Uses the primary voltage directly across the secondary resistor.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses the peak voltage to calculate mean power, doubling the result.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A wire connected to a d.c. power supply is positioned between the poles of a U-shaped magnet. The wire is at right angles to a uniform magnetic field between the poles and there is no field outside the poles. [Diagram: wire carrying 5.0 A passing between south and north poles of a U-shaped magnet; top view shows field lines from north to south across the wire.] When the current in the wire is 5.0 A, the force on the wire due to the magnetic field is 10 mN. The wire is now disconnected from the power supply. The wire is made to vibrate vertically with an amplitude of $1.8\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m}$ and a frequency of 90 Hz. The segment of wire between the poles remains horizontal during the vibration. [Diagram: wire vibrating vertically between the poles, dashed lines showing its extreme positions.] What is the maximum e.m.f. induced across the wire? A $0.32\ \mathrm{mV}$ B $2.0\ \mathrm{mV}$ C $0.32\ \mathrm{V}$ D $2.0\ \mathrm{V}$

stemImage.alt: Question 25: A wire connected to a d.c. power supply is positioned between the poles of a U-shaped magnet. You may assume that the wire is at right angles to a uniform magne

appearances.originalFile: NJC/H2 Physics/NJC_2026_H2_Physics_Prelim_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Combines F = BIL to find BL, SHM maximum speed, and motional e.m.f. BLv.
questions.misconception: Using amplitude or frequency directly as the speed instead of v0 = ωx0

explanation.body: From the force on the current-carrying wire, $B=F/(IL)$. The induced e.m.f. peaks at the maximum wire speed, $v_{\max}=\omega x_0=2\pi f x_0$. Thus $E_0=BLv_{\max}=(10\times10^{-3})(2\pi\times90)(1.8\times10^{-3})/5.0=0.00204\ \mathrm{V}$, or $2.0\ \mathrm{mV}$ to two significant figures.

perOption.A: Uses frequency in place of angular frequency and misses the factor of $2\pi$.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Misses the factor of $2\pi$ and reads the result in volts instead of millivolts.
perOption.D: Reads the numerical result in volts instead of millivolts.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A coil with N turns is placed in a uniform magnetic field. The area of the coil is initially perpendicular to the field, as shown in diagram (a). [Diagram (a): flat coil with ends X and Y, vertical field lines passing through it, axis of rotation in the plane of the coil.] The coil is rotated around the axis and the induced e.m.f. E between X and Y varies with time t as shown in diagram (b). [Diagram (b): sinusoidal E–t graph starting at zero, peaks $\pm E_0$, about two cycles.] $E_0$ is the magnitude of the maximum induced e.m.f. Which diagram best represents how E varies with t if the frequency of rotation is doubled and the magnetic flux density remains the same? The dotted line shows the graph in diagram (b) for comparison. [A: same frequency, larger amplitude. B: double frequency, smaller amplitude. C: double frequency, same amplitude. D: double frequency, double amplitude.]

stemImage.alt: Question 26: A coil with N turns is placed in a uniform magnetic field of flux density. The area of the coil is initially perpendicular to the field, as shown in diagram (a)

appearances.originalFile: NJC/H2 Physics/NJC_2026_H2_Physics_Prelim_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Needs E0 = NBAω so doubling frequency doubles both peak e.m.f. and frequency.
questions.misconception: Thinking only the frequency changes and the peak e.m.f. stays the same

explanation.body: The flux linkage is $NBA\cos(\omega t)$. Taking its negative time derivative gives $E=2\pi NBAf\sin(2\pi ft)$. Doubling $f$ doubles the peak e.m.f. to $2(2\pi NBAf)$ and halves the period.

perOption.A: Doubles the peak e.m.f. but keeps the original period.
perOption.B: Halves the period but incorrectly reduces the peak e.m.f.
perOption.C: Halves the period but keeps the original peak e.m.f.
perOption.D: Correct.

The bar magnet will

The bar magnet will A rotate in the opposite direction to the disc. B rotate in the same direction as the disc. C remain at rest. D oscillate to and fro in the horizontal plane.

options.label: B

questions.difficultyReason: Needs applying Lenz's law to eddy currents in an unfamiliar set-up.
questions.misconception: Expecting no interaction because aluminium is non-magnetic

explanation.body: By Lenz’s law, the eddy currents induced in the rotating disc oppose the change in magnetic flux through the disc. Their torque on the suspended magnet reduces the relative rotation, so the magnet turns in the same direction as the disc.

perOption.A: Opposite rotation would increase the relative motion driving the induction.
perOption.B: Correct. The induced torque drags the magnet in the disc’s direction.
perOption.C: Ignores the torque exerted by the induced currents.
perOption.D: Assumes a reversing torque even though the rotating disc initially drags the magnet in one direction.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A generator produces a current of 60.0 A r.m.s at a voltage of 120 V r.m.s. An ideal transformer steps up the voltage to a peak value of 4500 V and transmits the power through a cable of total resistance 40.0 $\Omega$ to the consumers. What is the percentage of power transmitted to the consumers? A 94.3 % B 97.2 % C 98.6 % D 99.3 %

stemImage.alt: Question 26: A generator produces a current of 60.0 A r.m.s at a voltage of 120 V r.m.s. An ideal transformer steps up the voltage to a peak value of 4500 V and transmits th

appearances.originalFile: NYJC/H2/2026 NYJC H2 Phy 9478 P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Chains transformer power, peak-to-r.m.s. conversion and $I^2R$ loss.
questions.misconception: Using the peak voltage instead of the r.m.s. voltage

explanation.body: The mean input power is $120(60.0)=7200\ \mathrm{W}$. The ideal transformer supplies the same power at $4500/\sqrt{2}\ \mathrm{V}$ r.m.s., so the cable current is $I_{\rm rms}=7200\sqrt{2}/4500\ \mathrm{A}$. After the cable loss, the power delivered is $P'=7200-I_{\rm rms}^2(40.0)$. The percentage delivered is $(P'/7200)\times100\%\approx97.2\%$.

perOption.A: Uses the peak cable current in the mean power-loss formula and doubles the loss.
perOption.B: Correct. About 97.2% of the power reaches the consumers.
perOption.C: Treats 4500 V as the r.m.s. voltage, halving the calculated cable loss.
perOption.D: Converts peak voltage to r.m.s. in the wrong direction by multiplying by √2, leaving only a quarter of the correct cable loss.

questions.stem:
The primary coil of a transformer is connected to an alternating voltage supply. The secondary coil is connected across a variable resistor.

Which change will cause an increase in the p.d. across the secondary coil?
questions.stemText: The primary coil of a transformer is connected to an alternating voltage supply. The secondary coil is connected across a variable resistor. 6.5 mV R primary coil secondary coil primary coil secondary coil Which change will cause an increase in the p.d. across the secondary coil? A decreasing the cross-sectional area of the secondary coil B decreasing the current in the primary coil C decreasing the resistance of the variable resistor D decreasing the number of turns of the primary coil

options.label: A
options.text: decreasing the cross-sectional area of the secondary coil

options.label: B
options.text: decreasing the current in the primary coil

options.label: C
options.text: decreasing the resistance of the variable resistor

options.label: D
options.text: decreasing the number of turns of the primary coil

appearances.originalFile: RI/H2/2026 RI H2Phy Prelims P1 Questions.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Applies the ideal transformer turns ratio at fixed input voltage.
questions.misconception: Treating load resistance as a control for ideal secondary voltage

explanation.body: For an ideal transformer, $V_s/V_p=N_s/N_p$. With $V_p$ and $N_s$ fixed, decreasing $N_p$ increases $V_s$.

perOption.A: Under the key's flux model, reducing the coil area reduces the induced e.m.f. $E=NBA\omega\sin(\omega t)$.
perOption.B: With $V_p$ and $I_s$ fixed, decreasing $I_p$ would decrease $V_s$ by $V_s/V_p=I_p/I_s$.
perOption.C: A smaller load resistance changes the secondary current while the ideal secondary voltage stays fixed.
perOption.D: Correct.

The resistance of the variable resistor is then gradually decreased to its minimum value, after which the switch is opened quickly.

At which stage is the magnitude of the current through the ammeter greatest?

The resistance of the variable resistor is then gradually decreased to its minimum value, after which the switch is opened quickly. soft iron A At which stage is the magnitude of the current through the ammeter greatest? A immediately after the switch is closed B while the resistance is being decreased C when the resistance reaches its minimum value D immediately after the switch is opened

options.label: A
options.text: immediately after the switch is closed

options.label: B
options.text: while the resistance is being decreased

options.label: C
options.text: when the resistance reaches its minimum value

options.label: D
options.text: immediately after the switch is opened

appearances.originalFile: RVHS/RVHS H2 Physics P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Compare how fast the flux changes at each stage in the two-coil circuit.
questions.misconception: Equating the largest primary current with the largest induced current

explanation.body: The primary current is greatest just before the switch opens, when the variable resistance is at its minimum. Opening the switch quickly then causes the greatest rate of change of magnetic flux through the soft iron. This gives the largest induced e.m.f. and hence the largest current through the ammeter.

perOption.A: The switch closes with the resistance at its maximum, so the change in primary current is smaller.
perOption.B: The gradual resistance change changes the flux more slowly.
perOption.C: Minimum resistance gives the largest steady primary current, but the secondary current depends on how fast the flux is changing.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A circular coil of area $300\ \mathrm{cm^2}$ is placed with its plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of $0.0500\ \mathrm T$. The coil has 50 turns and a resistance of $10.0\ \Omega$. It is connected to a circuit with a galvanometer with the circuit resistance also being $10.0\ \Omega$.

What is the quantity of charge that flows when the coil is suddenly removed out of the magnetic field?

A  $7.50\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm C$
B  $3.75\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm C$
C  $7.50\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm C$
D  $3.75\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm C$

stemImage.alt: Question 26: A circular coil of area 300 cm2 is placed with its plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.0500 T. The coil has 50 turns and a resistance of 10.0 Ω

appearances.originalFile: RVHS/RVHS H2 Physics P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Combine Faraday’s law with the current–charge relation and include both resistances.
questions.misconception: Using only the coil resistance or mis-converting square centimetres

explanation.body: Faraday’s law gives $\mathcal E=-\mathrm d(NBA)/\mathrm dt$. Using $\mathcal E=RI$ and $I=\mathrm dQ/\mathrm dt$ gives $R\,\mathrm dQ/\mathrm dt=-\mathrm d(NBA)/\mathrm dt$. The flux drops to zero, so the charge magnitude is $\Delta Q=NBA/R=\frac{50}{10+10}(0.0500)(300\times10^{-4})=3.75\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm C$.

perOption.A: This omits the circuit’s additional resistance and makes the converted area 100 times too small.
perOption.B: This makes the converted area 100 times too small.
perOption.C: This includes only one of the two $10.0\ \Omega$ resistances.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A soft-iron ring of variable cross-section has four coils wound round it at the positions shown. The coils have 2, 3, 4 and 5 turns. The 3-turn coil is connected to an a.c. supply.

In which coil does the magnitude of the magnetic flux density have the greatest variation?

[The ring has a 2-turn coil A at the wider lower-left section, a 3-turn coil B on the left connected to an a.c. supply, a 4-turn coil C at the narrowest section at the top, and a 5-turn coil D on the right.]

stemImage.alt: Question 26: A soft-iron ring of variable cross-section has four coils wound round it at the positions shown. The coils have 2, 3, 4 and 5 turns. The 3-turn coil is connecte

appearances.originalFile: SAJC - note P3 will be used for mock on 6 oct/2026 SAJC H2 Physics Prelim P1_for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: It requires distinguishing flux density from flux and flux linkage in a variable-area core.
questions.misconception: Confusing flux density with flux linkage

explanation.body: The same magnetic flux $\Phi$ passes through the soft-iron ring at all four coils. Since $\Phi=BA$, the variation in $B$ is greatest where the core area is smallest, at C. The number of turns affects the induced emf through flux linkage.

perOption.A: The wider core at A gives a smaller variation in flux density.
perOption.B: Being connected to the supply does not give B the smallest core area.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: The extra turn affects flux linkage, while D has a larger core area than C.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
The root mean square (rms) current in the primary coil of an ideal transformer is $2.0\ \mathrm{A}$. The rms voltage in the secondary coil is $50\ \mathrm{V}$. The average power transferred from the secondary coil is $20\ \mathrm{W}$.

What is $N_{\mathrm p}/N_{\mathrm s}$ and what is the average power transferred from the primary coil?

$N_{\mathrm p}/N_{\mathrm s}$ | Average power transferred from the primary coil / W
A $1/5$ | $4.0$
B $5$ | $20$
C $1/5$ | $20$
D $5$ | $100$

stemImage.alt: Question 27: The root mean square (rms) current in the primary coil of an ideal transformer is 2.0 A. The rms voltage in the secondary coil is 50 V. The average power transf

appearances.originalFile: SAJC - note P3 will be used for mock on 6 oct/2026 SAJC H2 Physics Prelim P1_for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: It combines power conservation, rms values and the transformer voltage ratio.
questions.misconception: Inverting the primary-to-secondary turns ratio

explanation.body: The ideal transformer has no power loss, so the primary transfers $20\ \mathrm{W}$. With the assumed unity power factor, $P_{\mathrm p}=V_{\mathrm p}I_{\mathrm p}$ gives $20=V_{\mathrm p}(2.0)$ and $V_{\mathrm p}=10\ \mathrm{V}$. The turns ratio is $N_{\mathrm p}/N_{\mathrm s}=V_{\mathrm p}/V_{\mathrm s}=10/50=1/5$.

perOption.A: Scales the power by the turns ratio, despite power conservation.
perOption.B: Inverts the turns ratio obtained under the unity-power-factor assumption.
perOption.C: Correct under the unity-power-factor assumption.
perOption.D: Uses the secondary voltage with the primary current and overstates the transmitted power.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
An aluminium disc of diameter d rotates about its centre. A point on the rim moves at a constant speed v. It is placed in a uniform magnetic field B perpendicular to its surface. A steady electromotive force (e.m.f.) E is generated between the centre O and the rim at P.

What is the expression for the e.m.f E generated?
questions.stemText: An aluminium disc of diameter d rotates about its centre. A point on the rim moves at a constant speed v. It is placed in a uniform magnetic field B perpendicular to its surface. A steady electromotive force (e.m.f.) E is generated between the centre O and the rim at P. P d O v What is the expression for the e.m.f E generated? A Bdv B 4 Bdv C 2 D Bdv Bv

appearances.originalFile: TJC/H2 Physics/2026 H2 Prelim Paper 1 final.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Students must relate rim speed to rotation frequency and then to the flux swept per unit time.
questions.misconception: Every point along the radius moves at the rim speed.

explanation.body: At the rim, $v=r\omega=2\pi fr$, so $f=v/(2\pi r)$. A radius sweeps an area $\pi r^2$ per revolution, giving $E=B\pi r^2f$. Substituting gives $E=Brv/2=Bdv/4$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Treats the entire radius as moving at the rim speed, giving $B(d/2)v$.
perOption.C: Uses the full diameter with the rim speed in the straight-conductor expression.
perOption.D: Omits a length factor, so the expression does not have units of voltage.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
An aluminum disc of radius $r$ rotates about its centre at a constant speed. The disc is placed is a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to its surface. A steady electromotive force (e.m.f.) $E$ is generated between the centre O and the rim at P.

[The disc rotates clockwise. P, Q, O and S are collinear from left to right, with P at the left rim and O at the centre. The distance from P to O is $r$.]

What is the e.m.f. generated between points Q and S, each a distance $\frac{r}{2}$ away from centre O?

A zero
B $\frac{E}{4}$
C $\frac{E}{2}$
D $E$

stemImage.alt: Question 26: An aluminum disc of radius r rotates about its centre at a constant speed. The disc is placed is a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to its surface. A steady

appearances.originalFile: TMJC/TMJC_2026_H2 Physics_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: The rotating disc requires tracking the radial dependence and sign of the induced e.m.f.
questions.misconception: Adding the two centre-to-point e.m.f. magnitudes along QOS.

explanation.body: For the rotating disc, the centre-to-rim e.m.f. is $E=BAf=B\pi r^2 f$. Q and S are both at radius $r/2$, where the enclosed area is one quarter of the disc area, so each centre-to-point e.m.f. has magnitude $E/4$. Along Q to O to S, the two radial e.m.f.s have opposite signs and cancel.

perOption.A: Correct. Q and S are at the same potential.
perOption.B: Gives the e.m.f. between O and either midpoint.
perOption.C: Adds the magnitudes along QOS even though the contributions have opposite signs.
perOption.D: Uses the centre-to-rim e.m.f. for two points at the same radius.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
The following circuit was set up to test a transformer. The input a.c. voltage $V_p$ is 450 V, with a current $I_p$ of 4.0 mA. The number of turns in the secondary coil, $N_s$ is 240 with a current $I_s$ of 120 mA.

[The primary coil $N_p$ and its ammeter are connected to the a.c. input $V_p$. The secondary coil $N_s$ has its own series ammeter and output terminals labelled $V_s$. The currents are labelled $I_p$ and $I_s$.]

The transformer was 100% efficient.

What is the number of turns in the primary coil, $N_p$ and output a.c. voltage, $V_s$?

Option | $N_p$ | $V_s$
A | 8 | 13500
B | 8 | 15
C | 7200 | 13500
D | 7200 | 15

stemImage.alt: Question 27: The following circuit was set up to test a transformer. The input a.c. voltage Vp is 450 V, with a current Ip of 4.0 mA. The number of turns in the secondary co

appearances.originalFile: TMJC/TMJC_2026_H2 Physics_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: One transformer ratio gives both requested values with straightforward arithmetic.
questions.misconception: Inverting the current ratio.

explanation.body: For the ideal transformer, $\frac{N_p}{N_s}=\frac{V_p}{V_s}=\frac{I_s}{I_p}=\frac{120}{4.0}=30$. Hence $N_p=30(240)=7200$ turns. The output voltage is $V_s=450/30=15\ \mathrm{V}$.

perOption.A: Inverts the current ratio for both the turns and the voltage.
perOption.B: Gets the voltage right but inverts the turns ratio.
perOption.C: Gets the turns right but multiplies $V_p$ by 30.
perOption.D: Correct. The primary has 7200 turns and the output is 15 V.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A plane heads East at a speed of $30\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, cutting the vertical component of the Earth’s magnetic field of flux density $B_v=5.0\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{T}$ acting downwards.

[A plane is shown with its nose pointing to the right. An arrow labelled as the vertical component of the Earth’s magnetic field, $B_v=5.0\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{T}$, points downwards.]

Taking the wingspan of the plane to be $17\ \mathrm{m}$, what is the e.m.f generated across the wing and which side of the wing will be at higher potential?

[Table columns are E.m.f generated / mV and Wing which is at higher potential.]
A 0, None
B 0.030, Left
C 26, Right
D 26, Left

stemImage.alt: Question 25: A plane heads East at a speed of 30 m s-1, cutting the vertical component of the Earth’s magnetic field of flux density Bv = 5.0 x 10-5 T acting downwards. vert

appearances.originalFile: VJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Find the motional emf and determine its polarity relative to the direction of flight.
questions.misconception: Reversing the direction of magnetic force on positive charge.

explanation.body: The motional emf is $\mathcal E=B_vlv=(5.0\times10^{-5})(17.0)(30)=0.0255\ \mathrm{V}$, which rounds to $26\ \mathrm{mV}$. For the polarity, the key uses Lenz’s law and Fleming’s left-hand rule to select the right-to-left direction for conventional current in the wing. The left wing is therefore at higher potential.

perOption.A: Misses the emf generated as the wing cuts the downward magnetic field.
perOption.B: Identifies the higher-potential wing but underestimates the emf from the given wingspan and speed.
perOption.C: Gets the emf magnitude but reverses its polarity.
perOption.D: Correct. The left wing is at higher potential.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A plane circular coil of 30 turns, each of diameter $1.0\ \mathrm{cm}$, rotates 1800 times each minute about a diameter which is perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of flux density $4.0\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{T}$.

What is the maximum instantaneous value of the induced electromotive force?

A $1.2\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{V}$
B $2.8\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{V}$
C $1.8\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{V}$
D $2.3\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{V}$

stemImage.alt: Question 26: A plane circular coil of 30 turns, each of diameter 1.0 cm, rotates 1800 times each minute about a diameter which is perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field o

appearances.originalFile: VJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Differentiate the flux linkage and use the coil area and angular frequency in SI units.
questions.misconception: Confusing frequency in hertz with angular frequency.

explanation.body: By Faraday’s law, $\mathcal E=-\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(NBA\cos\omega t)=\omega NBA\sin\omega t$. The maximum is therefore $(2\pi f)NBA$. Using $f=1800/60\ \mathrm{Hz}$ and $A=\pi(1.0\times10^{-2})^2/4\ \mathrm{m^2}$ gives $\mathcal E_{\max}=1.8\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{V}$.

perOption.A: Underestimates the peak rate of change of the total flux linkage.
perOption.B: Uses $f$ in place of $\omega=2\pi f$.
perOption.C: Correct. The peak emf is $\omega NBA$.
perOption.D: Overestimates the peak rate of change of the total flux linkage.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A magnetic field of uniform flux density $B$ is at an angle $\theta$ to the plane of a coil as shown.

[A perspective view shows a rectangular coil in a uniform magnetic field pointing to the right. A plan view shows the coil slanting up to the right at angle $\theta$ to the horizontal field lines.]

The coil has $N$ turns and the area of the coil is $A$.

What is the magnetic flux linkage of the coil?

A $BA\cos\theta$
B $BA\sin\theta$
C $BNA\cos\theta$
D $BNA\sin\theta$

stemImage.alt: Question 26: A magnetic field of uniform flux density B is at an angle  to the plane of a coil as shown. The coil has N turns and the area of the coil is A. What is the mag

appearances.originalFile: YIJC/2026 JC2 H2 Prelim Paper 1 QP (Revised).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: The expression follows once the normal component of the field is identified.
questions.misconception: Using the angle to the plane as the angle to the normal.

explanation.body: Multiply the number of turns $N$ by the field component normal to the coil and by the coil area $A$. Since $\theta$ is the angle to the plane, this gives $N\times B\sin\theta\times A=BNA\sin\theta$.

perOption.A: Uses the component parallel to the plane and omits the number of turns.
perOption.B: Calculates only the flux through one turn.
perOption.C: Uses $B\cos\theta$, the field component parallel to the plane.
perOption.D: Correct. It uses the normal field component and all $N$ turns.
